[THALABI:v7p7/r4] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | The original sense of nuṭfah is a small amount of water, and its plural is niṭāf.
[THALABI:v7p7/r5] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | An ʿalaqah is clotted, pure blood; its plural is ʿalaq.
[THALABI:v7p7/r6] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | A muḍghah is a small piece of flesh, about the size of a morsel one can chew.

[THALABI:v7p8/r1] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | The earth is inert, dry, and stripped of traces of crops and plants, like a fire gone out.
[THALABI:v7p8/r2] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | When rain falls, the earth stirs with vegetation, swells, and grows, increasing its plants with the coming of rain.
[THALABI:v7p8/r3] THALABI, d. 427 · أبو جعفر | reports | Abū Jaʿfar reads rabāʾat with hamzah, as also in 41:39; it means rose, increased, or swelled, related to Arabic for rising to a prominent place and the term for a scout. | mentions 41:39
[THALABI:v7p8/r4] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | The revived earth grows every beautiful kind of plant.
[THALABI:v7p8/r5] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | The revived earth demonstrates that God is the Real, revives the dead, has power over all things, and will raise those in the graves at the coming Hour.

[MAWARDI-FULL:v4p8/r12] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · ابن جريج | reports | Ibn Jurayj says it means dry and unable to grow anything.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v4p8/r13] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | reports | A third explanation takes هامدة as worn-out or barren, citing al-Aʿsha's line about clothes that are faded and worn.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v4p8/r14] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · الكلبي | reports | Al-Kalbi interprets اهتزت as “grew.”
[MAWARDI-FULL:v4p8/r15] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | reports | Alternatively, the plants themselves sway, with their movement becoming vigorous; a poem compares it to a branch in green leaves.

[MAWARDI-FULL:v4p9/r3] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · ابن شجرة | reports | Ibn Shajara interprets each زوج as each kind or species.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v4p9/r4] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | reports | Another possibility is every color, since plants vary in green, red, and yellow.

[WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p257#2/r1] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · أبو إسحاق | reports | Abū Isḥāq says the deniers should reflect on their beginning: divine power does not differ between initiating creation and restoring it.

[WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p257#2/r3] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · صاحب النظم | reports | The author of al-Naẓm paraphrases the argument: if you doubt resurrection, God informs you that He created you from dust.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p257#2/r4] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | Here the sperm-drop means the child of Adam, formed from the father’s semen; Arabic calls a small amount of water nuṭfa.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p257#2/r5] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | Nuṭfa derives from dripping: it can mean a clear remnant of water, a cloud’s dripping, or rain lasting through the night; semen is so named because it drips.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p257/r1] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās takes the address as directed to the people of Mecca.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p257/r2] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · أبو إسحاق | reports | Abū Isḥāq says the verse addresses polytheists who denied resurrection and were in doubt about it.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p258/r1] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | ʿAlaqa is thick, congealed blood before it dries, and a piece of that blood; the cited al-Qaṭāmī line witnesses the word ʿalaq.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p258/r2] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | The drop that forms a child thickens into blood; when the clot becomes flesh it is a muḍgha, a piece of flesh, as the human heart is a bodily morsel.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p258/r3] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās glosses muḍgha as flesh.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p258/r4] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | reports | A hadith cited here says each stage lasts forty days—drop, clot, then morsel—after which an angel is sent to breathe in the spirit.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p258/r5] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās says the fetus is formed during the ten days after four months, then receives the spirit; this explains the widow’s four months and ten days of waiting, and movement signals pregnancy.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p259/r1] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · ابن الأعرابي | reports | Ibn al-Aʿrābī says mukhallaqa is a stage whose form has begun to appear, while ghayr mukhallaqa has not yet been shaped.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p259/r10] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | prefers | He takes mukhallaqa here as fully created through the breathing of the spirit: a fetus completed alive goes to term, while miscarriage is incomplete in this sense.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p259/r2] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | The author identifies Ibn al-Aʿrābī’s explanation of mukhallaqa as the word’s lexical sense.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p259/r3] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · مجاهد | reports | Mujāhid, in Ibn Nujaḥ’s transmission, says the words describe miscarriage: a miscarried fetus is both formed and unformed.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p259/r4] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · السدي | reports | Al-Suddī details the miscarriage stages: a woman may miscarry a drop, a clot, unformed flesh, partly formed flesh, or a fully formed fetus.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p259/r5] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | He supports the miscarriage interpretation by reading ‘We establish in wombs what We will’ as what reaches its full term rather than being miscarried.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p259/r6] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās says mukhallaqa is what lives and ghayr mukhallaqa is miscarriage.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p259/r7] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · مجاهد | reports | Mujāhid, in Khusayf’s transmission, identifies mukhallaqa as the child and ghayr mukhallaqa as miscarriage.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p259/r8] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās, in ʿAṭāʾ’s transmission, says the formed fetus is one for whom the covenant was taken, whereas the unformed one had no covenant and is not created.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p259/r9] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · عبد الله بن مسعود | reports | Alqama reports from Ibn Masʿūd that an angel asks whether the drop is formed; if not, the womb expels it, but if so, the angel records sex, provision, lifespan, and destiny from the Preserved Book.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p262/r1] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · الكلبي | reports | Al-Kalbī glosses the pair as created and uncreated: a full-term child is created, and miscarriage is uncreated; the author says this is most commentators’ view and notes Abū ʿUbayda agrees.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p262/r2] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · قتادة | reports | Qatāda understands mukhallaqa and ghayr mukhallaqa as complete and incomplete; Abū Isḥāq and Thaʿlab choose this interpretation, which concerns born children rather than miscarriage.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p262/r3] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · أبو إسحاق | reports | Abū Isḥāq says some morsels complete their human organs and faculties, while God does not complete the formation of others.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p262/r4] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · أبو العباس | reports | Abū al-ʿAbbās says people are of two kinds: fully formed or deficient and incomplete.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p262/r5] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | On the third interpretation, mukhallaqa means complete in bodily form and limbs; the author summarizes three interpretations of mukhallaqa.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p264/r1] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās says the purpose is to show people what they should do and leave, and to distinguish the best of them and what worship requires.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p264/r10] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · صاحب النظم | reports | The author of al-Naẓm treats ونقر as a new independent statement after the clause ending at لنبين لكم, explaining its indicative mood.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p264/r2] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · الزجاج | reports | Al-Zajjāj says the stages of human creation demonstrate God’s power to do as He wills and inform people how He first created them.

[BURSEVI:v6p3#3/r8] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | God created people through these remarkable stages to clarify resurrection: whoever first created humans from lifeless dust can restore them.
[BURSEVI:v6p3#3/r9] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The cited couplets make the same inference: the One able to create people initially has manifest power to resurrect them.
[BURSEVI:v6p3/r1] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Strive day and night to purify the soul and subdue denial: this greater struggle faces the inward enemy that is hardest to evade.
[BURSEVI:v6p3/r2] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The author asks God to protect from enemies and make people follow the clear truth from which there is no deviation.
[BURSEVI:v6p3/r3] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The address is to the people of Mecca who deny resurrection.
[BURSEVI:v6p3/r4] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Baʿth means bringing people out of the earth and conveying them to the gathering place.
[BURSEVI:v6p3/r5] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The conditional إن appears despite many doubters because the evidence here uproots doubt and frames it as merely hypothetical.
[BURSEVI:v6p3/r6] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Doubt concerns either whether restoration is possible and within God’s power, or whether resurrection will occur.
[BURSEVI:v6p4#2/r1] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Those who die are taken by God after reaching maturity or before it; tawaffī denotes death and the taking of the soul.
[BURSEVI:v6p4#2/r2] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Ardhal al-ʿumr is decrepit old age and senility; ʿumr is the span during which life animates the body.
[BURSEVI:v6p4#2/r3] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The phrase describes a severe reversal of knowledge and condition: the elderly may forget what they did and knew and lose abilities, though they still know some things like a child.
[BURSEVI:v6p4#2/r4] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · الشيخ سعدي | reports | Saʿdī’s verses lament that youth and the season of life pass, warning that desire and play consume the years and youth does not return.
[BURSEVI:v6p4#2/r5] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · النسفي | reports | Al-Nasafī says ignorance before knowledge is hell because it breeds greed, whereas ignorance after knowledge is paradise because it brings acceptance and contentment.
[BURSEVI:v6p4#2/r6] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · البقلي | reports | Al-Baqli reads the worst age inwardly as striving after witnessing and spiritual interruption after communion, when one loses awareness of lofty states and stations.
[BURSEVI:v6p4#2/r7] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · البقلي | reports | Al-Baqli calls this God’s protective jealousy toward realized people who disclosed His secrets through excessive claims, and seeks refuge from the ego.
[BURSEVI:v6p4#2/r8] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · التأويلات النجمية | reports | The Taʾwīlāt al-Najmiyya says created beings rested in the wombs of nonexistence by God’s determination, each emerging only by His will at its anciently appointed term.

[BURSEVI:v6p4/r10] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | At the end of the fixed term, God brings people out from their mothers’ wombs.

[BURSEVI:v6p4/r14] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The purpose of reaching maturity is coordinated with the purpose of bringing people out: they grow gradually to adulthood.
[BURSEVI:v6p4/r15] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Reaching full strength means completeness in power, reason, and discernment, usually between thirty and forty.

[ALUSI-FULL:v17p115#2/r1] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The verse presents proof to silence disputants after warning of their end; people here most likely means unbelievers who dispute and deny resurrection.
[ALUSI-FULL:v17p115#2/r10] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | An ʿalaqah is a formed piece of clotted blood, and a muḍghah is a piece of flesh formed from it, about the size of what can be chewed.

[ALUSI-FULL:v17p116/r3] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · عبد الله بن مسعود | reports | Ibn Mas'ud reports that an angel asks God whether the settled semen is to be formed; if so, the angel asks its sex, fortune, lifespan, provision, and place of death. The report is treated as Prophetic.

[ALUSI-FULL:v17p117/r4] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · يعقوب | reports | Yaʿqūb reads نَقَرُّ with fatḥa on nūn and ḍamma on qāf, from a verb meaning to pour water.
